newsitem.title: FRANCE: French artists fight far-right mayor over theatre.
newsitem.headline: French artists fight far-right mayor over theatre.

text.p: Some 4,000 French artists and supporters marched through the southern city of Toulon on Thursday to combat a drive by an extreme-right mayor to sack a left-wing theatre director and wind up his cultural centre.
The arts establishment has clashed repeatedly with the anti-immigration National Front in the party's four southern bastions, denouncing censorship in libraries and at cultural events.
Some 200 singers, actors and film-makers took a night "Freedom Train" to the Mediterranean port to fight the dismissal of director Gerard Paquet by mayor Jean-Marie Le Chevallier.
"I cannot accept the diktat of a party...What is happening is typical of a totalitarian or fascist state attacking culture and freedom," rock star Jacques Higelin said.
"The first act of fascism is always to attack culture. There comes a time when you have...to call a fascist act a fascist act," award-winning film-maker Bernard Tavernier said.
The artists, including film director Claude Chabrol, comedian Guy Bedos and actor Roger Hanin, demonstrated in Freedom Square and attended a court hearing on the sacking.

The hearing began in a tense atmosphere but shortly afterwards was adjourned until March 27 at the request of Le Chevallier, who argued that the board running the theatre might appoint a successor to Paquet on Friday.

Laywers for the theatre and cultural centre at Chateauvallon said Paquet's sacking was illegal and denounced what they called a game played by Le Chevallier, regional prefect (government representative) Jean-Charles Marchiani, and Henri Nespoulous, appointed administrator of the centre.

The artists planned to stage another demonstration at Chateauvallon but Le Chevallier requested that it be banned. Paquet, after a series of clashes, was sacked for failure to get mayoral approval for printing the programme for 1997.

The newspaper Le Monde hailed a new mobilisation by French artists and intellectuals. "The Front's growth...and the far-right's stance which influenced the government's plans against immigration, have at last knocked the idea of an intelligentsia cut off from the realities of society's crisis," it said in an editorial.

Chateauvallon became a symbol of opposition to the Front when Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy and writers protested there late last year against Le Chevallier's ban on a tribute to Jewish writer Marek Halter.

The human rights group LICRA denounced "cultural and social censorship" by Front mayors for introducing far-right literature into municipal libraries, ending subsidies to associations helping immigrants, and stopping menus without pork at Marignane schools to penalise Moslem and Jewish children.

The opposition Socialist Party, reeling after the Front's victory in municipal elections in Vitrolles on Sunday, rushed to overhaul its Marseille-based apparatus in the Bouches-du-Rhone region, its stronghold in the 1970s.
Socialist leaders summoned local party bosses to Paris after the Front defeated outgoing mayor Jean-Jacques Anglade, under judicial investigation for alleged sleaze.
Spokesman Francois Hollande said the party, in the run-up to general elections due early next year, would present "exemplary candidates" with no question marks over their honesty.
Several of the film-makers in Toulon had on Wednesday sparred with a government minister, urging people to disobey hardline anti-immigration laws.

Some 150 writers, including Bernard-Henri Levy, Jean Lacouture, and best-selling Marie Darrieussecq, signed the filmmakers' appeal which urges civil disobedience against a law requiring French citizens to report the arrival and departure of foreigners staying at their home.
